about: Every algorithm of People World, one line each, in the order of the explainer steps. Line numbers are at the commit in base; build.mjs follows them to the current commit by matching the line text.

algorithms.name: Floyd–Warshall distances
algorithms.what: All-pairs shortest paths over the border graph, where a link is 0.86 times the two countries' radii added.

algorithms.name: Classical MDS
algorithms.what: Starting positions from the leading eigenvectors of the double-centred squared distances, found by power iteration with deflation.

algorithms.name: Stress majorization (SMACOF)
algorithms.what: Moves the discs until their distances match the graph distances, each pair weighted by 1/d².

algorithms.name: Constraint projection
algorithms.what: Position-based packing: linked discs overlap a little, unlinked ones are pushed apart, and a weak pull keeps the continent compact.

algorithms.name: Neighbour lists with hot discs
algorithms.what: Skips pairs that cannot touch. Each disc keeps a list of the others within reach, and only discs that have moved far since are checked against everything.

algorithms.name: Link uncrossing sweep
algorithms.what: Two links drawn as crossing segments can't both be borders, so the cheaper endpoint is pushed back across. Candidate pairs come from a sweep over bounding boxes, merged with a min-heap.

algorithms.name: Link difficulty scores
algorithms.what: How many other links each link crosses, and how stretched it is. Among equally small sets of exclaves, the solver drops the hardest links and those of the smallest countries.

algorithms.name: Continent orientation
algorithms.what: The main continent is turned to lie along its long axis and the second stands upright beside it; mirroring varies with the seed.

algorithms.name: Left-Right planarity test
algorithms.what: Brandes' linear-time test: DFS orientation, lowpoints, nesting depths and conflict pairs, written iteratively over typed arrays.

algorithms.name: Counting sort of edges
algorithms.what: Stable bucket sorts give each vertex's edges in nesting-depth order in linear time.

algorithms.name: Planar embedding & faces
algorithms.what: Builds the rotation system (neighbours in counter-clockwise order) and traces every face. Each component satisfies V − E + F = 2.

algorithms.name: Biconnected blocks
algorithms.what: Iterative Hopcroft–Tarjan with an edge stack. Only the blocks that are not planar get any more work.

algorithms.name: Kuratowski extraction
algorithms.what: Finds an edge-minimal K₅ or K₃,₃ subdivision by group deletion: drop a chunk of edges, keep it dropped if the rest is still non-planar, otherwise split the chunk.

algorithms.name: 2-core pruning
algorithms.what: Edges of pendant trees never belong to a Kuratowski subgraph, so they are dropped for free after every deletion.

algorithms.name: Implicit hitting set
algorithms.what: Minimum planarizing edge deletion. Every answer removes an edge of each Kuratowski subgraph, so collect them, find a cheapest hitting set, test it, add what it misses, and repeat until it is proven optimal.

algorithms.name: Branch and bound
algorithms.what: Searches hitting sets under degree, disjoint-packing and LP-dual weight lower bounds. The count is minimised first, then the weight.

algorithms.name: Dominance & union-find
algorithms.what: Drops superset constraints and dominated edges, then splits the problem into independent parts with union-find.

algorithms.name: Euler bound
algorithms.what: A planar graph has at most 3n − 6 edges (2n − 4 with no triangles), which bounds the number of removals from below.

algorithms.name: Greedy planarization
algorithms.what: Takes the edges in order and binary-searches the longest planar prefix; the edge that breaks it is dropped and the search goes on.

algorithms.name: 2-for-1 exchange search
algorithms.what: When the time budget runs out: put two removed edges back and remove one other, as long as the graph stays planar.

algorithms.name: BFS-local deletion order
algorithms.what: Edges far from a centre (by BFS distance) are deleted first, so extracted subgraphs stay small and local and make strong constraints.

algorithms.name: Graded jittered quadtree
algorithms.what: About 50,000 points from a quadtree on a fixed lattice, finer where small countries sit. A grid over the discs answers the sizing queries.

algorithms.name: Position-hashed jitter
algorithms.what: Each point's jitter is a hash of where it is, so wherever the countries are the same, so is the mesh.

algorithms.name: Delaunay triangulation
algorithms.what: Mapbox's Delaunator: a sweep-hull Delaunay triangulation of the points.

algorithms.name: Robust orient2d
algorithms.what: Shewchuk's adaptive-precision orientation test: a quick floating-point answer when it is provably right, exact arithmetic when it is not. Delaunator uses it for its hull walks; its in-circle test, which decides the flips, is plain floating point.

algorithms.name: Barycentric dual
algorithms.what: Each cell is the triangle thirds around a point (centroid to midpoint to centroid), which is always a valid planar subdivision.

algorithms.name: Capped growth from seeds
algorithms.what: Every country's front advances at a speed set by its size and stops at its target area. Small countries keep a round blob; big ones flow around them.

algorithms.name: Power diagram start
algorithms.what: An alternative start, off by default: each cell goes to the seed with the least power distance d² − r², clipped to noisy discs.

algorithms.name: Potts energy
algorithms.what: Border length, plus area error, plus distance from the country's centre, plus a coast noise field, plus a spring on borders that are still too short.

algorithms.name: Metropolis annealing
algorithms.what: Proposes for each boundary cell the label of a random neighbour and accepts it by the Metropolis rule as the temperature falls. A move must pass both the energy test and the hard rules; the cheaper energy test runs first.

algorithms.name: Simple-point test
algorithms.what: Checks the cell's ring of neighbours, so a country stays in one piece, never gets a hole, and the sea gets no new lake.

algorithms.name: Position-keyed random order
algorithms.what: Cells are visited in hash order and draw their random numbers from (key, sweep), so where the map is the same it anneals the same way.

algorithms.name: Active frontier set
algorithms.what: Only cells on an edge between labels are visited; a cell inside one country cannot change anything.

algorithms.name: Dijkstra on Dial's buckets
algorithms.what: Cheapest-path distance fields on a bucket queue, with the same result a binary heap would give.

algorithms.name: Binary min-heap
algorithms.what: A heap of (key, cell) pairs over typed arrays, used by growth, bridging, blob growing and channel broadening.

algorithms.name: Border bridging
algorithms.what: Two countries that must touch grow arms toward each other along the cheapest legal path; the corridor is then widened by a ring of cells.

algorithms.name: Reinsertion
algorithms.what: Takes a country that is stretched, or still missing a border, off the map and grows it again where the most neighbours are close and no forbidden country is near. buildWorld keeps the result only if it helps.

algorithms.name: Exclave carving
algorithms.what: Cuts a detached piece of one country out of its host: inside it, on the border of two hosts, or in the sea against its coast.

algorithms.name: Arm pruning
algorithms.what: Cells farther than k·R from the country's thickest point go to a neighbour that may take them, or to the sea.

algorithms.name: Morphological opening
algorithms.what: Removes ribbons and necks: keep the cells at least r deep, grow them back by r, and give away whatever is not covered.

algorithms.name: Channel broadening
algorithms.what: Long water channels between countries that must not touch become broad seas with noise-shaped shores, and are then frozen.

algorithms.name: Inlet filling
algorithms.what: One-cell inlets and narrow creeks are filled from the tip with the land around them, where the rules allow.

algorithms.name: Component cleanup
algorithms.what: Keeps one connected piece per country (the one with its seed) and resolves any contact between countries that are not linked.

algorithms.name: Boundary chain graph
algorithms.what: The labelled cells become a planar graph of chains between the junctions where three labels meet.

algorithms.name: Uniform segment grid
algorithms.what: A dense grid of segment lists over the map, kept current as vertices move.

algorithms.name: Guarded vertex moves
algorithms.what: Every move is tested against nearby segments: no crossing, no pinch, no fold to zero width. The topology settled on the mesh survives everything after.

algorithms.name: Displacement budgets
algorithms.what: A vertex may move at most half of the room left between its segments and the nearest boundary it must keep clear of, so no gap closes below its clearance. Blocks of 16 segments with bounding boxes skip the pairs that cannot lower any budget.

algorithms.name: Incremental gap pushes
algorithms.what: Finds vertices too close to a boundary they must keep clear of, rechecking only where something moved.

algorithms.name: Neck detection
algorithms.what: Off by default: two sides of one country that are close in space but far apart along its outline are a neck, and are pushed apart.

algorithms.name: Taubin smoothing
algorithms.what: A shrinking Laplacian step, then an inflating one, so small blobs keep their size.

algorithms.name: Segment subdivision
algorithms.what: Splits every segment longer than a share of its chain's mean segment length (half on coasts, 0.8 on borders), so the roughening has points to bend. The matching simplify, which drops vertices on nearly straight runs, is never called.

algorithms.name: Fractal roughening
algorithms.what: Moves vertices along the normal by fBm noise: coasts get capes and coves, borders a gentle wobble.

algorithms.name: Exact area fitting
algorithms.what: Pushes each chain toward the side with too much area, with a gain per country, until every area is within tolerance. The sea absorbs the difference.

algorithms.name: Radial collapse
algorithms.what: Shrinks a tiny country toward a point it is star-shaped from. Its neighbours take the strips, and their borders extend along the rays.

algorithms.name: Curve-shortening flow
algorithms.what: When a tiny country is not star-shaped, plain Laplacian steps on its own outline (8 at a time, its junctions held) straighten it, and collapse is tried again, up to 8 attempts. Only a country with no junctions, a closed loop inside one neighbour, gets the full flow toward a convex shape.

refs.label: plain steps when Taubin is off

algorithms.name: Despike & spur cutting
algorithms.what: Hairpin vertices move to their neighbours' midpoint, and hairline loops are cut off with a straight segment.

algorithms.name: Junction straightening
algorithms.what: Where a border meets the sea, the coast is pulled onto a chord so it runs straight on instead of dipping into a V.

algorithms.name: Gap opening
algorithms.what: Pushes apart the boundaries of countries that must not look as if they touch, until each pair keeps its clearance.

algorithms.name: Exact-area blobs
algorithms.what: Low-frequency lobes plus detail, a little elongated, then rotated and scaled to exactly the right area.

algorithms.name: Expanding-ring search
algorithms.what: Largest island first, each one searches rings of growing radius around its anchor for the first free spot.

algorithms.name: Open-water placement
algorithms.what: A piece of land of its own (Britain and Ireland) goes to the open water nearest its continent's middle, with a straight way out to sea.

refs.label: the fallback round the main land

algorithms.name: Pull-back layout
algorithms.what: After an edit each country is pulled back toward where it was, so a change fades with distance.

algorithms.name: Incremental planarity
algorithms.what: The earlier exclaves are kept, and each new link becomes a border if the map stays planar with it.

algorithms.name: Fresh-build fallback
algorithms.what: An edit that breaks a rule or takes too long is drawn again from scratch, and the page says that countries moved.

algorithms.name: Scanline rasterization
algorithms.what: An even-odd fill of every country's rings: which country each cell's middle lies in.

algorithms.name: Pocket filling
algorithms.what: A flood fill: pockets of no country inside the land go to the country most round them, so no river ends in a sliver.

algorithms.name: Euclidean distance transform
algorithms.what: Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher's exact EDT in two one-dimensional passes: how far every cell lies from the sea.

algorithms.name: Disc stamping
algorithms.what: Distance to nearby sources only, by stamping a disc around each. Cheaper than a transform of the whole grid.

algorithms.name: Line marking & dabs
algorithms.what: Marks the cells a line passes through in steps of a third of a cell, and lays smooth bumps on a field, which keeps the larger of the bump and what it had.

algorithms.name: Fixed lattice
algorithms.what: Cell sizes come from a series a quarter of a doubling apart, anchored at the origin, so a map that changes a little keeps its cells.

algorithms.name: Rough inland relief
algorithms.what: The ground rises with distance inland, roughened by fBm. Every border stands on a low ridge, higher where three meet, so rivers cross borders at saddles.

algorithms.name: Border ranges
algorithms.what: Some long borders get a range on one side, its crest a little way in, as the Pyrenees follow theirs.

algorithms.name: Priority-flood
algorithms.what: Floods from the sea inward with a binary heap, giving every land cell a way down with no pits.

algorithms.name: Flow accumulation
algorithms.what: Rain is passed down the drainage tree from the highest cells to the lowest, and more of it falls on the heights.

algorithms.name: Divides into ranges
algorithms.what: Mountains stand on the divides between two sizeable basins, on their highest stretches, with each country's share capped.

algorithms.name: River extraction
algorithms.what: Cells that gather enough flow are rivers, drawn largest first. Where two meet, the larger runs on and the smaller ends on its line.

algorithms.name: Shared domain warp
algorithms.what: Every point is pushed by a slow wave and a quick one, the same push for every river, so courses bend together and keep their junctions. A check afterwards cuts a river at any crossing, so no two cross.

algorithms.name: Catmull-Rom splines
algorithms.what: A smooth curve through the river's points (cell middles, pushed by the warp and averaged three times), four points to a cell.

algorithms.name: Chaikin corner cutting
algorithms.what: One pass of corner cutting after a small wave along the river's course.

algorithms.name: Range breaching
algorithms.what: Where a river passes through a range, the range gets a gap as wide as the valley.

algorithms.name: Valleys by flow
algorithms.what: Soft dabs every half cell along each river, wider and deeper with its flow: the valley it would have cut, without simulating erosion.

algorithms.name: Wandering wind belts
algorithms.what: Trades, westerlies and polar easterlies, with still calms between them that wander north and south. Half the worlds spin the other way.

algorithms.name: Upwind moisture trace
algorithms.what: From each land cell the air is followed back upwind to the sea, then forward again: it fills over water and rains out over land.

algorithms.name: Orographic rain shadow
algorithms.what: Air that climbs rising ground drops more rain; the lee of a range stays dry.

algorithms.name: Temperature with height
algorithms.what: Warm in the south, cold in the north and colder with height; the isotherms bend with the sea air.

algorithms.name: Whittaker biome table
algorithms.what: Warmth and moisture pick what grows (tundra, taiga, steppe, grassland, forest, scrub, desert, savanna, jungle) and how much of the ground is under trees.

algorithms.name: Equalized woodland noise
algorithms.what: Patch noise squashed so it spreads close to evenly over 0 to 1, so a threshold of cover puts about that share of the ground under trees.

algorithms.name: Marsh detection
algorithms.what: Low, wet, flat ground near the sea or at a river's mouth.

algorithms.name: Repeated box blur
algorithms.what: A box blur over land only, run twice: a tent-shaped filter that smooths the traced moisture.

algorithms.name: Seaward extrapolation
algorithms.what: Each ring of sea cells takes the mean of its neighbours that already have a value, so fields read at the coast stay the land's.

algorithms.name: Per-world question hash
algorithms.what: A MurmurHash3-style mix of the world number and a question, so neighbouring world numbers get different climates.

algorithms.name: Pole of inaccessibility
algorithms.what: The largest empty circle inside a country, where its name goes. Grid refinement, inside tests from crossings sorted per row, and a tree of boxes that gives up on a point once it cannot win.

algorithms.name: Ranked Douglas–Peucker
algorithms.what: Every point is ranked once for all tolerances, so a new zoom level only filters instead of simplifying again.

algorithms.name: Greedy colouring
algorithms.what: Countries with the most neighbours go first, each taking the first of seven colours its coloured neighbours lack. After an edit a country keeps its old colour unless a neighbour coloured before it already has it.

algorithms.name: Level of detail & culling
algorithms.what: Lines stay within 0.4 px of the full outline at the current zoom, and only lines on screen get new detail.

algorithms.name: Marker decluttering
algorithms.what: Where the rings for tiny countries crowd, only the biggest country of a cluster keeps its ring.

algorithms.name: Time slicing
algorithms.what: Long jobs run in slices of about 12 ms, yielding through a MessageChannel, which background tabs do not slow down.

algorithms.name: Bitmap gesture preview
algorithms.what: During a pan or pinch the drawn picture moves as one image; the paths are drawn again when the gesture rests.

algorithms.name: Hit testing
algorithms.what: The land under the pointer, or else the nearest marker within reach.

algorithms.name: Search ranking
algorithms.what: Two rankers, accents and case folded. Enter takes an exact name, then a beginning or a part only one country has, then a two-letter code. The suggestions list beginnings, then word beginnings, then from three letters any part, with a matching code on top.

algorithms.name: Base-62 edit codes
algorithms.what: Each border edit packs into four base-62 characters (two country codes and add or cut), so a long session fits in a link.

algorithms.name: FNV-1a text key
algorithms.what: A dropped DOT file is named in the address by a 32-bit FNV-1a hash of its text.

algorithms.name: Learned progress estimate
algorithms.what: The share of build time before each progress mark starts from built-in figures and is replaced by the last finished build's own timings for the rest of the visit. It paces the bar between marks and gives the time left.

algorithms.name: Zoom-band tile pyramid
algorithms.what: Square tiles anchored to the world, one set per doubling of zoom, shown at 0.71 to 1.41 times their scale. Tiles drawn apart meet without a seam.

algorithms.name: Worker pool & LRU cache
algorithms.what: One or two workers draw tiles on OffscreenCanvas, and each keeps its last 100 tiles as PNGs.

algorithms.name: Colour-coded raster survey
algorithms.what: Each country is drawn in a colour that spells its index; an EDT then gives every cell its distance to the sea, the land and the nearest border.

algorithms.name: Per-realm quotas
algorithms.what: Each realm gets thresholds of its own, so no more than a share of it lies under hills or woods.

algorithms.name: Widest open water
algorithms.what: Finds the widest stretches of sea, with room to each side, for the compass rose, the ship, the serpent and the sea names.

algorithms.name: Perlin noise
algorithms.what: Seeded gradient noise and its fractal sums, for the style's own downs and forest stands.

algorithms.name: Maximin colours in CIELAB
algorithms.what: The most constrained realm first takes the paper farthest from its neighbours' (lightness counted double), then two passes improve the worst pairs.

algorithms.name: Principal-axis name fit
algorithms.what: Second moments of the outline give its long axis, and the largest font that fits along it is found.

algorithms.name: Parabolic baselines
algorithms.what: A parabola fitted to the middles of the crossings bends a name along its land; a great realm's name is arched a little.

algorithms.name: Back-to-front woods
algorithms.what: Woods are drawn in bands from the back, so the trees in front hide the feet of those behind: the painter's algorithm.

algorithms.name: Simplify & segment grid
algorithms.what: Douglas–Peucker outlines and lines at 0.3 px of each band's zoom, and a uniform grid of segments that says whether a border or coast is near: it keeps marks off borders and coasts, and stops a river being drawn along a border.

algorithms.name: Banded point-in-polygon
algorithms.what: A country's edges sorted into horizontal bands, for fast inside tests.

algorithms.name: Country-ID pass
algorithms.what: The GPU first draws which country each pixel belongs to, exact to the pixel.

algorithms.name: Segment distance fields
algorithms.what: A quad around each border segment gives the exact distance in every pixel, and MAX blending joins them into one field with round joins.

algorithms.name: Derivative-damped fBm
algorithms.what: Inigo Quilez's erosion-like noise: the ridged octaves are damped by the slope built so far. The octaves follow the zoom and fade in and out.

algorithms.name: Value noise with gradients
algorithms.what: Quintic value noise that also returns its analytic derivative, carried through as dual numbers.

algorithms.name: Bicubic B-spline sampling
algorithms.what: Four bilinear texture reads make one bicubic B-spline sample, so the fields stay smooth at any zoom.

algorithms.name: Imhof-style shading
algorithms.what: Light from the northwest with warm lit slopes and cool shadows, plus snow, rock, beaches and cliffs.

algorithms.name: Whittaker colour lookup
algorithms.what: A 32 × 32 table of ground colour and forest cover by warmth and moisture.

algorithms.name: Hashed crowns & lights
algorithms.what: Tree crowns and lights sit in hashed grid cells per zoom level and fade between levels, so a zoom spreads them and never shuffles them.

algorithms.name: Strip repaint on pan
algorithms.what: A pan shifts the last frame by whole pixels and paints only the new strips.

algorithms.name: Ear-clipping triangulation
algorithms.what: Mapbox's earcut, with z-order hashing, triangulates every country for the GPU.

algorithms.name: Shelf & distance fields
algorithms.what: A scanline raster, an EDT for distance inland and out to sea, and three box blurs (close to a Gaussian) for the shallows.

algorithms.name: DSATUR colouring
algorithms.what: The most constrained country is coloured first, each preferring the slot its code hashes to, so colours survive most edits.

algorithms.name: Mulberry32 PRNG
algorithms.what: Seeded random numbers: the same world number always gives the same map.

algorithms.name: Integer hash
algorithms.what: A number in [0, 1) from three integers, behind every choice that is keyed to a position.

algorithms.name: Value noise & fBm
algorithms.what: Smooth lattice noise, summed over octaves.

algorithms.name: Bit-exact hypot
algorithms.what: Math.hypot as V8 computes it (scaled by the larger, Kahan-summed): the same bits in every browser, and faster than the builtin.

algorithms.name: Segment predicates
algorithms.what: Orientation, proper crossing and segment-to-segment distance, used to keep boundary lines from crossing or pinching when their vertices move.

algorithms.name: Shoelace area
algorithms.what: The signed area of a polygon ring.

algorithms.name: DOT tokenizer & parser
algorithms.what: A hand-written parser for Graphviz files: chains, subgraphs, scoped defaults, ports and HTML ids.

algorithms.name: PageRank
algorithms.what: Power iteration (damping 0.85, 100 rounds) with links read both ways sizes the nodes that carry no size of their own.

algorithms.name: Size attribute detection
algorithms.what: Picks the first size attribute that most nodes carry as a positive number and that tells them apart.

algorithms.name: Measure scaling
algorithms.what: Scales land area or GDP so the sizes add up to the world's people. A GDP that neither the World Bank nor tools/gdp-others.json has is the population times the median GDP per person.

algorithms.name: Rule checker
algorithms.what: Builds worlds in Node and checks the three rules, with every area within 1% of its share.
